messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 54-year-old civil servant who lives with his girlfriend, Elena. Three years ago, he left a long-term relationship with a man who, over the final year, subjected him to repeated physical assaults. The worst episode happened in their bedroom: an argument over finances escalated, and his partner pinned him to the bed, forearm across his throat. David could not breathe; he tasted copper—his own blood from a split lip—and the ceiling above him blurred into a series of still images, each one frozen and precise, like photographs clicked in sequence. He stopped fighting and went limp, and afterwards the memory of that night did not come back as a continuous story. When he deliberately tried to recall it, only fragments emerged, but the taste would return unbidden—metallic, sharp—and with it came the photographic images he could not control.

Now, David avoids being alone with men. At work, when a male colleague closes his office door for a private discussion, David’s chest tightens. He keeps his own door open and schedules meetings in open-plan areas or conference rooms with glass walls. The loss of control he experienced during the abuse has become a generalised dread: any situation where he feels trapped or powerless, even a crowded elevator, sends his mind reeling back to that bedroom. Sleeping alone—if Elena works late or travels—is unbearable; the empty bed triggers the taste memory and the photographic flash of the ceiling, and he will call friends or stay up until dawn rather than lie still.

To cope, David has developed a set of strategies that keep him moving. He detaches from the memories: when a flash surfaces, he mentally narrates his current surroundings in a flat, clinical tone, refusing to let the images feel real. He also keeps himself constantly surrounded by people. After work he volunteers for committees, attends every social event, and often invites neighbours over in the evening. Being alone in a room, even for a few minutes, feels dangerous—the taste might come, and then the photographs. The constant socialising is exhausting, but it works in the moment.

Yet the strategies themselves create new problems. The more he detaches from his memories, the harder it becomes to access them deliberately—he now relies on fragmentary flashes that arrive without warning, and the deliberate gaps make the unexpected intrusions feel more alien and threatening. And the constant socialising means he is almost never alone with his thoughts, but it also means he is frequently in the presence of men—colleagues, neighbours, friends’ partners—and each encounter heightens his hypervigilance. When a male coworker claps him on the shoulder, David’s stomach drops; he feels the loss of control all over again, and the taste floods his mouth.

The cycle tightens. At home, Elena has noticed that David cannot sit through a quiet evening. He fills the silence with podcasts or invites people over, and when she asks why he seems afraid of their own apartment, he deflects. He has come to believe that if he stops moving, if he lets himself be alone, the memories will crush him—that the taste and the photographs will become so vivid he will relive the choking. What finally drove him to seek help was a panic attack during a performance review: his male boss praised his work, and David, feeling pinned by the attention and the closed door, lost all sense of where he was. He excused himself, trembling, and the taste of blood stayed in his mouth for the rest of the day. Now he sits in a therapist’s office, hoping to find a way to let the memories exist without running from them, but terrified that slowing down will only bring the photographs back for good.
